papers.note: The canonical bias survey, with three taxonomies covering metrics, datasets and mitigation stages.
papers.title: Bias and Fairness in Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models are powerful AI systems that generate human-like text, but they can inadvertently learn and spread unfair biases from their training data. This survey examines how to identify these biases and fix them. The authors created three organizational frameworks covering how to measure bias, what test datasets exist to catch it, and what techniques can reduce it at different stages of model development. Understanding these problems matters because these systems increasingly influence important decisions affecting real people's lives.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying large language models face risks from embedded social biases that can harm users and create legal exposure. This survey provides a structured framework for understanding bias problems and solutions across the entire model lifecycle. Decision makers should use these taxonomies to evaluate which mitigation strategies fit their development stage and risk tolerance. The consolidated datasets enable systematic testing before deployment. Understanding these categorized approaches helps organizations implement fairness as a technical requirement alongside performance metrics, reducing reputational damage and ensuring systems treat all users equitably.
papers.explain_practitioner: This comprehensive survey consolidates bias evaluation and mitigation approaches for large language models through three taxonomies. The evaluation metrics taxonomy organizes assessment methods by operational level: embeddings, probability distributions, and text generation. The dataset taxonomy categorizes bias testing resources by structure and targeted harms while providing consolidated access to public benchmarks. The mitigation taxonomy classifies intervention techniques across four stages: preprocessing, in-training, intra-processing, and post-processing, with detailed subcategories. The work synthesizes recent research to clarify methodological relationships and identify research directions for reducing harmful bias propagation in language models.

papers.note: Early work defining representational bias sources and pushing the performance fairness frontier rather than trading one off.
papers.title: Towards Understanding and Mitigating Social Biases in Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models, which power many AI systems used in healthcare and law, can unintentionally learn and spread harmful stereotypes about gender, race, and religion from their training data. This paper identifies where these biases come from, creates tests to measure them, and develops techniques to reduce bias while keeping the AI systems working well. The researchers show their approach successfully removes unfair stereotypes without making the systems less capable.
papers.explain_business: This work addresses a critical risk for organizations deploying language models in consequential domains like healthcare and legal services, where biased outputs could cause real harm. The paper provides practical measurement tools and mitigation techniques that reduce stereotype propagation without sacrificing model quality. This enables responsible deployment while maintaining competitive performance, reducing regulatory and reputational risk.
papers.explain_practitioner: We systematized sources of representational bias in pretrained language models and developed new benchmarks and metrics for quantification. We then proposed mitigation strategies for bias during text generation. Our approach, validated through both automatic metrics and human evaluation, achieves bias reduction while maintaining high-quality output and contextual fidelity, advancing the Pareto frontier between fairness and performance objectives.

papers.note: Separates intrinsic from extrinsic bias and organises evaluation by data, model and output level.
papers.title: Bias in Large Language Models: Origin, Evaluation, and Mitigation
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models, the AI systems behind chatbots and writing tools, tend to absorb biases from their training data and can make unfair decisions. This paper explains where these biases come from, how researchers can detect them, and what techniques can reduce them. Understanding this matters because biased AI affects real people in critical areas like healthcare and the criminal justice system, so building fairer AI requires knowing how to spot and fix these problems.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying language models in high-stakes domains face legal and reputational risks from algorithmic bias. This paper provides a structured framework for identifying where bias enters systems and which interventions work best at different stages. For executives, it clarifies that bias management requires investment across the entire pipeline, from data curation through post-deployment monitoring. Selecting appropriate mitigation strategies now prevents costly failures and regulatory issues later while building customer trust in AI-driven decisions.
papers.explain_practitioner: This review categorizes bias in LLMs as intrinsic, originating from training data and model architecture, or extrinsic, arising from deployment context. The authors systematize evaluation approaches across three levels: examining training data for problematic patterns, analyzing model weights and behaviors, and assessing final outputs for discriminatory results. They survey mitigation techniques applied before training, during training, and after deployment, evaluating each approach's strengths and limitations to guide practitioners selecting appropriate interventions for their specific bias concerns.

papers.note: Splits fairness work by model scale and training paradigm, which matters when advising on fine tuning versus prompting.
papers.title: A Survey on Fairness in Large Language Models

papers.note: Summarises evaluation metrics plus the toolkits and datasets available to run them, a practical starting kit.
papers.title: Fairness in Large Language Models: A Taxonomic Survey
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models are powerful AI systems, but they can unfairly discriminate against certain groups of people, especially marginalized communities. This paper surveys what fairness means for these systems, how to measure when they're behaving unfairly, and what methods can make them fairer. It also catalogs practical tools and datasets researchers can use to test whether their models treat everyone equally.
papers.explain_business: Deploying language models without fairness safeguards risks legal liability, reputational damage, and customer harm through discriminatory outputs. This reference consolidates evaluation metrics, testing tools, and proven techniques for identifying and reducing bias. Executives can use it to understand what fairness means operationally, what resources exist to audit models, and what remediation strategies are available before deployment.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey synthesizes current work on fairness in large language models, covering bias sources, fairness definitions specific to LLMs, evaluation metrics, and mitigation algorithms. It catalogs available toolkits and datasets for bias assessment, distinguishing fairness challenges in LLMs from traditional machine learning contexts. The work provides a structured taxonomy of existing approaches and identifies open problems to guide development of fair LLM systems.

papers.note: 22 of 24 studies found bias, with gender bias in 15 of 16, the clearest prevalence evidence for medical deployments.
papers.title: Evaluating and addressing demographic disparities in medical large language models: a systematic review
papers.journal: International Journal for Equity in Health
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers reviewed studies on whether medical artificial intelligence systems treat people fairly across different groups. They found that 22 out of 24 studies discovered bias, with the strongest evidence showing these systems favor one gender over another. While researchers are getting better at spotting bias, they are still struggling to fix it effectively. This matters because these systems increasingly help doctors make treatment decisions, so unfair outcomes could harm patients from underrepresented groups.
papers.explain_business: Medical organizations considering deploying large language models should recognize that existing systems demonstrate persistent demographic biases affecting clinical recommendations. Current mitigation approaches like prompt adjustments show limited effectiveness, meaning bias risk remains high. Organizations deploying these tools face regulatory, ethical, and liability concerns if systems produce disparate patient outcomes. Investment decisions should account for ongoing research needs and the immaturity of bias correction techniques. Leadership should prioritize implementation in lower-stakes applications until bias mitigation technology matures significantly.
papers.explain_practitioner: We conducted a systematic review of 24 peer-reviewed studies examining demographic biases in medical large language models across five databases from 2018 to 2024. Quality assessment used Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Results showed 91.7% of studies identified bias, with gender bias appearing in 93.7% of gender-focused studies and racial or ethnic bias in 90.9% of studies examining these factors. Most mitigation attempts relied on prompt engineering with inconsistent results. Publication bias likely inflates prevalence estimates. The findings indicate widespread bias detection capability but insufficient mitigation solutions.

papers.note: Finds performance on commonsense tasks varies by culture and by the language the question is asked in, which is a concrete measurement of a bias usually discussed abstractly.
papers.title: Understanding the Capabilities and Limitations of Large Language Models for Cultural Commonsense
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested whether large language models, like chatbots, understand common sense the same way across different cultures. They found these systems perform better on some cultural tasks than others, and surprisingly, they work differently depending on what language you ask the question in. This matters because it shows AI systems have hidden biases that favor certain cultures, which could lead to unfair or unhelpful responses for people from underrepresented groups.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying language models must recognize that these systems perform inconsistently across different cultural contexts and languages. This has direct implications for global applications, customer service, and content moderation. Companies should conduct culture and language specific testing before deployment, expect variable quality in different markets, and plan localization strategies rather than assuming one model works equally well everywhere.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study evaluated large language models on cultural commonsense reasoning tasks across multiple cultures and languages. Performance varied significantly based on both the cultural context of the task and the language used for questioning. This demonstrates that model capabilities are not uniform across cultural domains and that language choice influences task performance, indicating that cultural representation in training data and evaluation methodologies requires careful consideration.

papers.note: Digital ageism is rarely covered elsewhere, and this mitigates it without touching model parameters.
papers.title: Mitigating Age-Related Bias in Large Language Models: Strategies for Responsible Artificial Intelligence Development
papers.explain_beginner: This research tackles a hidden problem: artificial intelligence systems sometimes treat older people unfairly or give them worse results than younger people. The scientists created a method called FairLLM that helps AI systems recognize and fix these age-related mistakes without rebuilding the system from scratch. The solution uses techniques inspired by human empathy, teamwork between multiple AI systems, and human oversight to make the AI more aware of its biases and generate fairer responses for people of all ages.
papers.explain_business: Age bias in AI systems creates legal, reputational, and fairness risks for organizations deploying language models in customer-facing applications. This work demonstrates a practical framework that improves fairness outcomes without expensive model retraining or replacement. For executives, the parameter-free approach means faster implementation and lower technical barriers to adoption. The cooperative bias detection model suggests scalability across different deployment scenarios. Organizations can reduce exposure to digital discrimination claims while improving user experience across demographic groups, particularly benefiting underserved older populations.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper presents a two-stage bias mitigation framework addressing age-related discrimination in LLMs through parameter-free mechanisms. The approach employs two operational modes: autonomous self-assessment where models identify and correct their own age biases, and cooperative modes leveraging multi-model consensus through debate. A key innovation is the empathetic perspective exchange strategy, which reframes context to generate age-appropriate responses. Evaluation on multiple datasets shows FairLLM substantially reduces age bias metrics compared to baseline methods, utilizing reinforcement learning and human-in-the-loop validation throughout the pipeline.

papers.note: Prices fairness breaches against the AI Act fine tiers using 12.4 million real underwriting records, a rare quantified case.
papers.title: Algorithmic Bias Under the EU AI Act: Compliance Risk, Capital Strain, and Pricing Distortions in Life and Health Insurance Underwriting

reading.body:
Large language models absorb biases from their training data and propagate them in deployment, with medical systems showing bias in 91.7% of evaluated studies and gender bias appearing in 93.7% of gender-focused cases.

The research separates bias into intrinsic sources, which originate in data and model architecture, and extrinsic sources, which emerge during deployment. Evaluation frameworks now organize detection across three levels: training data patterns, model weights and outputs, and real-world results. Mitigation techniques span preprocessing, in-training, intra-processing, and post-processing stages, each with documented tradeoffs. The field has moved from identifying whether bias exists to cataloging how to measure it and where in the pipeline to intervene. This matters because bias in consequential domains like medicine and criminal justice directly harms real people, and organizations face regulatory exposure, reputational damage, and liability when systems produce disparate outcomes.

The data does not show which mitigation techniques work best overall. Medical studies found that prompt engineering, the most common intervention attempted, showed inconsistent results. One framework achieves age bias reduction without retraining, suggesting parameter-free approaches can work, but prevalence and generalization remain unclear. Cultural commonsense performance varies by both culture and question language, indicating that bias measurement itself depends on context and design choices in evaluation. The research consolidates taxonomies and toolkits for testing, but the practical frontier between fairness and performance remains contested across papers and application domains.
